operations.name: Basic Surface Attack | Tactical Pattern
operations.narrative: This Sinai training sortie combined general airmanship, formation work, and CCIP range employment for five pilots across two airframes. The formation element was anchored by Sword (71.5 min) and XTC (53.5 min) as the apparent leads, with MeGaTron, PushMaster, and TITAN completing abbreviated 17–18 minute range sorties. The standout positive of the day is TITAN's weapons performance: 3 shacks from 5 passes, including a 0.8 m CEP near-perfect hit on run 3, representing the best single-pass result recorded in recent squadron history and a dramatic reversal from two consecutive F-grade BVR missions. MeGaTron showed the most consistent release parameters and lowest avgCEP (17.4 m) of the three CCIP pilots, with one shack, though a stubborn SHORT bias across four passes must be corrected. PushMaster submitted six passes but posted zero shacks, an avgCEP of 49.7 m, and a catastrophic 152.3 m outlier on run 5 — a bomb that would have been a friendly-fire incident in a real CAS environment. The formation data for PushMaster is equally concerning: 11 breakaways, avgJoinSec 143 s, and 52% of tracked time outside any recognised formation — a sharp regression from his August A-grade. The most serious safety finding of the entire sortie is XTC's 20.8 g spike at 01:15:39, flagged as a HIGH_G_INSTANT during a routine transit phase on the FA-18C whose structural limit is +7.5 g. This is an unacceptable exceedance that would ground the aircraft and trigger a mandatory safety investigation in any professional squadron. Sword flew the longest and smoothest sortie with maxG 5.3 and zero exceedances, but the absence of any weapons employment across 71.5 minutes is a missed training opportunity. Release altitudes across the CCIP group trended low — TITAN's minimum of 1,622 ft AGL and MeGaTron's 1,761 ft final pass both approach the frag-safety floor for BDU-50LD class weapons. The squadron must enforce a hard floor of 2,000 ft AGL for training CCIP passes. Overall, one brilliant weapons performance, one developing, one failed, one missing, and one safety emergency define this sortie.
lessons: CCIP SHORT bias correction: if four of five passes are short, do not adjust the aiming point — extend the dive, verify the CCIP solution is fully computed before release, and resist the instinct to pull off early. The pipper tells you when to press the pickle button, not your gut.

Formation rejoin discipline is non-negotiable: an avgJoinSec of 143 s means the wingman was a liability for over 2 minutes per gap — in a threat environment this gets the element killed. Every breakaway must be followed by an aggressive, deliberate rejoin with the lead monitoring and calling the closure.

G-awareness is a survival skill: a 20.8 g transient on the Hornet during routine transit is a structural failure event. All pilots must brief their personal G-limits, recognise when inputs are becoming abrupt, and consciously manage stick forces — especially during low-altitude manoeuvring and recovery from CCIP runs.

The package collectively achieved 6 ground kills out of a possible 8, which represents a partial success. Sword led Viper and drew first blood at T+49:09 with an Mk-82 on a HEMTT soft target, then followed up with a gun kill on a TPZ armour unit at T+01:10:24 — the only pilot to employ both bomb and gun against different target classes, demonstrating flexible employment. operations.name: BFM and BVR Practice
operations.narrative: The Sinai training mission ran from 02:11 to approximately 03:01, encompassing five BFM rounds and five A-A/BVR rounds across all four pilots. In BFM, [EAF] MeGaTron dominated comprehensively: he defeated [EAF] PushMaster in Rounds 1 and 4/5, and Golden_Pilot in Round 3, converting neutral positions to gun saddle via superior energy management in the turning fight. PushMaster was consistently unable to hold an offensive position against MeGaTron — 0% offensive time in Round 1, 19% in Round 4 despite firing 423 rounds for zero hits, a clear indication that he is pulling the trigger from outside a valid firing solution. Both BFM pilots committed multiple deck busts (MeGaTron 2–3 per slot, PushMaster 2 per slot) and racked up sustained over-G events that are the primary safety concern of this debrief. The transition to BVR at Round 6 reshuffled the hierarchy: Golden_Pilot emerged as the session's most lethal pilot with 5 kills, including tight-parameter shots at 2.1–9.8 nm. PushMaster found his form in BVR, scoring 4 kills with patient, close-range employment. MeGaTron struggled in BVR, going 1-for-3 in kills while dying repeatedly — his BFM instinct to close to guns does not translate well when he needs to manage radar picture and employ BVR missiles at optimal range. ToRnAdO joined the BVR fight and showed flashes of competence (the 39 nm kill on PushMaster in Round 7) but died four times and recorded a structural G exceedance of 10.83 G in the final slot that demands immediate attention from the maintenance authority. Formation discipline was universally poor — no pilot maintained meaningful formation during BVR, with Golden_Pilot recording a 323 s rejoin time in one slot and ToRnAdO's early-round discipline scores near zero. The blue team won the BVR series 3-1, but margin of victory was narrow and both teams left significant Pk on the table through long-range launches. The recurring theme across all four pilots is trigger discipline and G discipline — both require immediate corrective focus before the next live weapons sortie.
lessons: G discipline is a life-and-death issue, not a score metric: MeGaTron recorded 9.93 G and 4 ft minAGL; ToRnAdO hit 10.83 G — both pilots must complete an immediate G-awareness ground school and review OBOGS/G-suit serviceability before flying again. There is no kill worth a structural failure at 2,000 ft AGL.

BVR trigger discipline: the red team averaged launches at 15–40 nm with sub-10% Pk; blue team closed to 7–12 nm before firing and achieved splashes. The lesson is simple — hold fire until the geometry gives you a sub-1,000 m CPA probability, not when the radar first goes active.

Formation standards exist in BVR too: a 2-ship that spends most of a 5-minute engagement with the wingman 7,800 m out of position (Golden_Pilot slot 5) is a 1-ship — the second aircraft provides no mutual support, no target separation, and no tactical flexibility. All pilots must practise the rejoin to within 30 s or the formation authority is degraded.

operations.name: Formation Practice
operations.narrative: Sword flight launched on the Sinai map for a dedicated formation training sortie with three F-16Cs and one dissimilar FA-18C. Megatron and Hema joined within 13 seconds of each other at T+05:58 and T+06:11 respectively; KAF joined 4 minutes 43 seconds late at T+10:41. The sortie immediately revealed a critical asymmetry: only Hema's formation module produced tracking data, while Megatron and KAF registered zero formation ticks for their entire flights — meaning two-thirds of the flight generated no measurable formation discipline output. Hema, flying the Ibraheem slot, delivered an outstanding 84-minute formation performance anchored by a final discipline score of 98.55/100, with fingertip as the dominant position (52% of 5,040 tracked ticks) and productive exposure to echelon right (28%), route (7%), and trail (6%). His 96 formation type changes across the sortie demonstrate active engagement with the instructor's formation transitions. The only blemish was a formation break sequence at T+36:29 and T+37:48 where separation grew from 136 m to 1,097 m with a -496 ft altitude differential — a rejoin that was sluggish and must be corrected. Megatron flew a full 84-minute sortie with disciplined G-management (maxG 5.01, 0 exceedances) but produced no formation tracking data; his 2,291 corner-speed ticks suggest independent manoeuvring rather than wing work. KAF compounded the formation deficit by joining late, recording a 6.72 G peak of unexplained origin outside any formation context, and departing 23 minutes before the flight concluded. Both Megatron and KAF must resolve why their formation modules produced no output — whether a position issue, a tracker configuration problem, or genuine absence from the formation stack. The minAGL readings of 7 ft (Megatron and Hema) and 9 ft (KAF) require instructor clarification; if no low-level profile was briefed, these figures represent safety floor violations. On balance, Hema carries this sortie with a genuine B-grade formation performance; the other two pilots leave the debrief with process questions rather than training credit.
lessons: Formation tracking coverage is non-negotiable on a formation training sortie — if two of three wingmen generate zero formation ticks, the training value of the flight is halved. Pilots must brief and verify formation tracker activation before departure, and leads must confirm geometric proximity to the reference aircraft throughout.

A formation break that grows from 136 m to 1,097 m in 79 seconds indicates insufficient power response on rejoin — when separation exceeds 500 m in close formation, an immediate burner or military power correction is required, not a gradual closure. Hema must drill emergency rejoin power management.

Punctuality and sortie commitment are airmanship standards: a 4-minute-43-second late join and a 23-minute early departure (KAF) disrupt the flight's training programme for all members. The standard is to be airborne and in position before lead taxis, not after.

operations.narrative: Round 8 was a 1-v-1 BVR training engagement on the Sinai map, blue ({EAF} Omar) versus red ([EAF] TITAN), lasting 415 seconds and ending with a blue win by side destruction. The engagement opened with Omar already committed from a prior exchange against [EAF] 9g | Sword — two misses at 22.8 nm and 36.3 nm — before TITAN spawned at 22:59:06 and the scored round began at 23:04:37. Both pilots prosecuted the merge at medium-to-high altitude (avg ~29,000–30,000 ft) with speeds in the 730–760 kt range. TITAN fired all three of his shots from beyond 25 nm (35.3, 35.6, and 31.8 nm), averaging 35.45 nm — every round a free Pk gift to Omar, who defeated them at CPAs of 17,399 m, 14,342 m, and 7,110 m respectively. TITAN compounded the error by never cranking after a shot (crank time = 0 s), spending 260 of 386 defending seconds flying hot and presenting a predictable aspect. Omar's kill came at 23:03:37 when he pressed inside 11 nm and rippled two AIM-120Cs — the first connected at CPA 76 m (SPLASH, TOF 21 s); the second was already airborne and marked TARGET_DOWN_MIDFLIGHT as TITAN ejected at 23:03:53. In the subsequent reset TITAN landed a retaliatory shot on Omar at 31.8 nm (CPA 139 m, SPLASH), ultimately killing Omar at 23:11:12 — however, Omar had already departed the server at 23:10:47 per the tracker FINISH record, so this kill fell outside the scored round window and is not credited in Omar's facts. The tactical lesson is the same for both pilots: launch range discipline is the primary failure. Omar's sole scoring shot at 11 nm is proof of concept — when he closes to parameters, the weapon works. TITAN's structural G of 8.9 G (1 sustained flag) is borderline; Omar's 15.8 G with five instant spikes is a serious airmanship failure that must be addressed before any further weapons employment training. MinAGL of 117 ft for Omar is a near-CFIT event that cannot be repeated. Both pilots show improving trends in their history, but the weapons employment fundamentals — launch gates, post-launch cranking, notch quality — need deliberate rehearsal before progressing.
lessons: LAUNCH GATE DISCIPLINE: Neither pilot fired a scoring shot inside 20 nm consistently. Set a hard mental gate — do not pickle AIM-120C beyond 20 nm against a manoeuvring, aware target; inside 15 nm the Pk rises dramatically as TOF drops below 30 s and defeat geometry collapses. Omar's 11 nm shot (TOF 21 s, CPA 76 m) is the template.

POST-LAUNCH CRANK: TITAN recorded 0 seconds of crank time across all three shots, flying hot and predictable for the entire missile flight — this maximises the target's defeat geometry and removes any post-launch Pk benefit. After every shot, immediate 45–60° beam turn to increase antenna train angle and complicate the threat's notch solution; sustain until terminal.

G DISCIPLINE AND ALTITUDE AWARENESS: Omar's 15.8 G and 117 ft AGL are unacceptable even in a training arena. The F-16C's structural limit is 9.0 G; pulling to the stops in a defensive break is a technique failure, not a solution. Combine threat reaction with altitude deconfliction — never allow the floor to creep inside 2,000 ft AGL during manoeuvring flight.

operations.name: SinaiMap 2026-10-18 22:06Z BVR practice
operations.narrative: Two EAF F-16C pilots flew a 1v1 BVR training sortie on Sinai map across two formal rounds plus extended free-play. Round 15 lasted only 69 seconds and was aborted KIO with no kills; Round 16 ran 180 seconds and ended with Omar scoring a kill before TITAN withdrew. In Round 1 (23:29 timeline), both pilots opened hot at long range — Omar fired first at 18.5 nm (miss, CPA 237 m), then fired an egregious shot at 41.2 nm which the tracker ultimately credited TARGET_DOWN_MIDFLIGHT only because TITAN died to other ordnance while the missile was still in flight — not a genuine intercept kill. TITAN's sole offensive shot at 16 nm missed by 4,577 m, and his second shot went against an Unknown target for a further waste. Omar survived TITAN's 1 inbound missile easily (defeat CPA 4,577 m) but then bled energy to 295 kt at 8,197 ft and recorded a minAGL of -4 ft — a near-fatal deck bust immediately after the kill. In Round 2, Omar re-engaged from 68 nm, fired at 32.9 nm (another out-of-parameters shot, SPLASH but the target was not killed by that missile alone), then pressed in and fired a valid ripple at 10.6–12.9 nm which achieved the confirmed kill at 23:49:32. However, Omar then continued firing 4 more missiles at the already-dead target — pure panic ripple that wasted half a magazine. TITAN in Round 2 opened cold (ATA 142°) at 39.9 nm — tactically incoherent — then turned hot but was immediately put defensive by Omar's 32.9 nm shot and never recovered offensive posture, dying for the second time. The extended free-play phase saw Omar fire 6 more AIM-120Cs at Unknown targets between 24:07–24:09, all of which missed, suggesting unsupervised envelope exploration without structure. TITAN's overall performance — 0 kills, 2 deaths, 0 crank seconds, Pk 0% — reflects a pilot who has not yet internalised BVR offensive fundamentals. Omar's outcome (2 kills, 0 deaths) looks positive on the scoreboard but masks systemic shot indiscipline, a deck bust, zero notching, and a 7.1% overall Pk across 14 shots that cannot be accepted at EAF standards.
lessons: SHOT DISCIPLINE: Do not release AIM-120C beyond 25 nm against a manoeuvring target without a supporting geometry advantage (altitude, closure, aspect). Every shot beyond that band in this sortie either missed or was credited only because the target died to other ordnance in flight. Fire fewer missiles at higher-probability parameters; this sortie burned 14 AMRAAMs for 2 kills.

POST-LAUNCH GEOMETRY — CRANK AND NOTCH: TITAN never cranked once after launching, remaining hot and predictable for the entire sortie. Omar never notched during his 50 seconds of defending. Both pilots must build the crank-notch-re-engage sequence as reflex: after launch, turn 40–60° off the threat axis immediately; when inbound, place the threat at 90° to defeat the seeker. These are not optional — they are survival skills.

ENERGY RECOVERY AFTER DEFENSIVE: Omar's ENERGY_POOR flag at 295 kt / 8,197 ft and the -4 ft minAGL confirm that post-defensive recovery nearly killed him. The rule is unload to 1 G, select MIL/AB, and do not pull again until above corner speed (~450 kt). A BVR kill followed by flying into the ground is a tactical own-goal.

highlights: Both confirmed kills scored: Round 1 kill at ~18.5 nm (within 15–25 nm band, full context credit given kills were confirmed trackerside), Round 2 kill confirmed at 23:49:32 — survived both engagements with 0 deaths across 29 minutes of flight, demonstrating good overall survivability and defensive awareness (defeated 1/1 inbound, CPA 4,577 m).

Executed a crank of 118 seconds after Round 2 first shot at 32.9 nm, showing understanding of the post-launch geometry concept; re-engaged hot with enough energy (860–895 kt) for the final attack sequence.

Overall Pk across all 8 scored shots is 12.5% (2 kills / 8 shots) but only 2 of those shots were in an acceptable launch band; 14-shot total across the full session (including the later unknown-target practice) produced the same 2 kills — a 7.1% Pk that is unacceptable.

Energy management after a defensive manoeuvre must be a priority; recovering from a split-S or hard turn requires immediate unloading and mil power, not continued manoeuvring into the ground.

Managed to defeat 2 of 7 inbound missiles (avg defeat CPA 2,381 m), showing some awareness of incoming threats despite being struck once.

Spent 203 of 416 tracked seconds defending with zero offensive cranking — no crank time whatsoever. After going defensive, TITAN never re-entered the offensive, allowing Omar to control the entire engagement; died twice in 7.1 minutes of flight.

Study the AIM-9M/X minimum and maximum range envelope — do not fire at TOF under ~6 s (inside arming range) or at TOF over ~60 s against a manoeuvring target in the notch. Two credible shots beat eight wasted ones and preserve the magazine for a real opportunity.

operations.narrative: This was a mixed TRAINING/A-A/SEAD package that in practice became an all-SEAD strike on an SA-15 (TorM2) point-defence site — there was no air-to-air engagement recorded for anyone. The four-ship of F-16s plus a Hornet (KAF) rolled in against a layered SAM threat, and the standout lesson of the day is that only ONE HARM out of a dozen-plus launches actually killed the radar. Sword owns the sortie: he pressed the WEZ, absorbed the counterfire (defeated one SA9M338K, ate one hit and lived), and put an AGM-88 into the TorM2 radar at 10.0 nm for the flight's only confirmed kill — a clean reversal of his declining 33-44 trend. KAF put two HARMs on target with beautiful terminal CPAs of 85 m and 48 m from 14.5 nm, but his telemetry is corrupted with repeated 16-33 G spikes and 38 instant-G flags that read either as replay artefact or violently jerky stick work — no radar kill was credited to him. MeGaTron flew disciplined standoff shots in an 11-12 nm band but connected on only 1 of 4, a sharp effectiveness drop from his 104-point sortie last week. Neo had the worst day: 0 for 3 on HARMs including a wasted 15.7 nm lob and a 222-second time-of-flight shot fired far out of parameters, and his formation work collapsed — discipline of 61.9, average rejoin 87 seconds, a worst rejoin of 183 seconds, and 26% of the mission spent at 'none' separation (4000 m off). That is a stark regression from the 112-point formation mission he flew a week ago. Nayal flew the cleanest airmanship in the flight — maxG 1.3, no exceedances, formation discipline 82.6 — but only logged five minutes and contributed nothing offensively. Across the flight the layered-threat lesson held: the point-defence SA-15 fought back with SA9M338K shots and everyone survived only because Sword suppressed it. Nobody died, and no friendly kills occurred — the debrief.log shows only AI hit/kill spam with no attribution to our pilots. operations.narrative: This was a coordinated SEAD press against an S-300 (with two SA-15/TorM2 point-defence escorts) plus a Roland ADS battery, with the stated tactic of hitting the site from different angles and launching at similar distances — Viper element (Moataz) separating and Cobra staying together. The plan was sound and PushMaster executed it perfectly: a 12.6 nm HARM at 00:46:42 shacked the S-300 search radar (terminal CPA 189 m) for the only kill of the day, and both his shots impacted. That kill is the mission's high-water mark and validates the whole standoff concept. The rest of the flight illustrated exactly why the layered-threat lesson exists. MeGaTron, despite the best standoff range (21.5 nm) and the cleanest G, was the first man down at 00:45:22 to the S-300 tracker having never fired — good range is worthless without a shot in the air. Hema pressed to 10.0 nm with no HARM aboard at all and was killed at 00:46:19 inside a known WEZ, the doubled-loss scenario, capping a worrying decline (21→10). His 15G instant flag at 00:37:56 is a gross-overstress spike I want explained. Moataz flew a beautiful defensive — 100% against two 25 nm S-300 shots — but then dove to 6.5 nm and shot both HARMs from inside 8.5 nm, both misses. Neo dumped a 4-round HARM salvo from ~9 nm inside the TorM2 ring; all four missed with the best CPA at 1227 m, and his 10.1G flags show a jet flown right at the ragged edge. Sword had the second-best geometry (four shots 11-12 nm) and a 62 m near-miss that simply should have killed — a lock/handoff issue, not a discipline one. The tactic worked where it was flown as briefed (PushMaster) and failed where pilots either brought no ARM or pressed inside the point-defence envelope to shoot. Net: the concept is proven, the execution discipline is not yet there for five of six.

Never enter a SAM WEZ without an anti-radiation missile aboard — Hema pressed to 10 nm empty and died. That is the named no-ARM-inside-10nm penalty.

operations.narrative: This debrief covers ONLY the second SEAD sortie — Sword and Hema (Ibraheem) against 2x SA22 (Pantsir/Tor-type IR point defenders) that spawned around 01:45-01:48 and were engaged at roughly 02:11. Per directive I have set aside the first S-300 flight and the Blacksky/Kaf/Hesper/Amro package entirely. The briefed tactic was correct for a training environment: get low, accept deep WEZ penetration, and rifle HARMs in the 8-15nm band. Both pilots executed the ingress profile as briefed — low, fast, weapons away inside the window. Sword pressed to 8.4nm at 689kts and put one HARM into the site (cpa 183m), a clean on-parameter shot, and critically he lived. Hema shot first at 700kts but all four of his HARMs missed, the opener at 9.7nm sailing 4.6km wide — that is a ripple fired before a settled solution. The layered-threat lesson wrote itself: Hema pressed inside 7nm against an active Pantsir, defeated the first SA57E6 (cpa 1682m), then was struck by the second and killed at 02:12:04. Even under a permissive training ruleset, you shoot-then-defend; you do not loiter in the ring with no impacts on the board. Sword's shooting was better but still only 25% impacts, with three trailing missiles landing 388-588m off. Both jets showed ragged 9G+ spikes down at 800-900ft during the pickle passes — energy management on the shot needs work. Bottom line: Sword suppressed and survived; Hema neither killed the site nor came home. The difference between the two scores is the death in a known WEZ, which the rubric weighs heavily even in training.

Against SA22-class point defenders, sequence shoot-then-defend: get the weapon off and immediately break out of the ring — Hema defeated missile one but died to missile two by staying in the WEZ.
Trade the 9G+ deck-level pickle pulls for smoother energy — spiking to 9.4G at 880ft stresses the jet and degrades your own shot without buying separation.

operations.name: SEAD Training
operations.brief:
SEAD TRAINING 
2-SHIP SWORD AND MOATAZ VS SA10 + SA15
operations.narrative: This was a 2-ship SEAD problem against a layered SA-10 with an SA-15 point-defence escort at maximum lethality preset - the exact 'layered threat' scenario that punishes crews who only respect the long-range ring. Sword opened the attack at 00:23:50 with a four-round HARM ripple from 9.8-10.7 nm, and to his credit walked one down to a 259 m terminal miss - close, but every shot was scored MISS. Moataz followed at 00:27:31 with his own four HARMs, but fired them from 10.4-11.5 nm while sitting at 1173-3102 ft; those low, close shots all missed with a best CPA of 1307 m. The single biggest failure of the day is that ZERO radar kills and ZERO site kills were achieved - the SA-10 was never destroyed and never went silent for the 2-minute suppression credit, so eight HARMs bought nothing but noise. Where both pilots earned their keep was survival and defence: this was a saturated engagement with SA-5B55s and an SA-15 Tor all pointed at them. Moataz defeated 7 of 8 inbounds (87.5%), including the terminal SA-15 shot at 1217 m - respecting the point-defence layer is exactly the lesson this mission teaches, and he did it. Sword's defence was thinner, 2 of 3 with one missile getting through, though he too survived. Both crews pressed dangerously deep - Moataz to 6.6 nm and Sword to 8.6 nm - with 630 s and 628 s in the WEZ respectively, far too long for a site that was still shooting. The HARM technique is the root problem: low, fast, close launches instead of high, standoff lofts that let the seeker and the missile's kinematics do the work. Airmanship was at the limit throughout - both hit ~9.4 G with instant-G flags clustered in the defend windows, and both bottomed out at 7 ft AGL, which is a deck-bust I will not wave. Moataz's formation work was decent (86.8 discipline, best rejoin 10 s) but his 97 s worst-case rejoin and repeated FORMATION_BREAKs out to 4551 m show the flight came apart under pressure. Sword's formation telemetry never populated, so I cannot positively grade his station-keeping this go. Against the pilot history, Moataz continues his decline (89 to 65 to now sub-60) and needs to arrest it; Sword is holding around his recent SEAD level but has not converted. Bottom line: two live jets returned, but the SA-10 also survived - that is a failed suppression mission redeemed only by defensive discipline.
lessons: HARM standoff is everything: eight missiles fired from inside 11.5 nm at 1000-5000 ft all missed. Loft the HARM from higher and further so it arrives with energy - close, flat shots against an SA-10 are wasted rounds.
Respect BOTH layers: the SA-15 Tor terminal shot at 1217 m nearly killed Moataz. Point-defence escorts kill pilots who only plan against the long-range ring - keep the escort's WEZ in your picture.
WEZ exposure discipline: 630 s and 628 s inside a lethal ring with no kill to show is pure risk. Shoot from range, turn cold, and re-attack - do not loiter in the threat while your missiles miss.
Deck awareness under G: both pilots hit 7 ft AGL while defending at 9+ G. Set a hard floor and honour it - a defeated missile means nothing if you fly into the ground.

operations.name: Introduction to SEAD
operations.narrative: This was an 'EXCELLENT - max lethality' SA-10 preset with an SA-15 point-defence escort — the classic layered threat — and the honest headline is that the radar never died. Seven F-16s put roughly 21 HARMs and 4 JSOWs into the air across a five-minute window from 00:45 to 00:51, and every single one is logged as MISS. Not one radar kill, not one site suppression event of note, and the S-300 fire-control lived to fight another day. On the positive side, survival was 100%: nobody self-killed and nobody was struck, which in a max-lethality SA-10 arena is not nothing. Standoff discipline was actually good across most of the flight — Sword fired from 53-58nm, Hema from 42-47nm, Moataz from 48-58nm, Neo from 45-50nm, all well outside the WEZ. The failure was terminal accuracy: the tightest CPA all day was Moataz at 582m, and most shots landed 2-3km off, with Neo's two HARMs a catastrophic 18-20km wide. Hema was the tactical bright spot defensively, eating two S-300 (SA5B55) shots and defeating both cleanly at 12-14km CPA for a 100% defeat rate. Blacksky pressed hardest and worst — 161s in the WEZ, in to 27.8nm, with three misses and a worst rejoin of 1210 seconds. MeGaTron is the goat of the sortie: not a single weapon employed, yet 103s of WEZ exposure — that is risk banked for zero return. Formation discipline was poor overall: Blacksky sat 'none' 59% of the time and Hema 69%, with only Moataz posting a respectable disc score of 72. Rejoins were glacial — 1210s, 1659s, 508s — nowhere near the sub-30s a tight wingman owes his lead. And Hema's G-trace is a serious flag: nine HIGH_G_INSTANT events including logged spikes of 24.3G and 32.7G with min speed of 34kts, which either means departures/overcontrol or a corrupt sensor, and I want it investigated before next brief. Bottom line: good posture, catastrophic conversion — the primary SEAD objective failed.
lessons: A SEAD sortie is graded on the radar dying, not on missiles fired — 25 shots, zero kills means the mission failed. Fix HARM employment geometry: proper HAS/pre-briefed handoff, correct range/altitude, and lock before launch (Neo's 18-20km CPA and everyone's 2-3km misses say the solutions were wrong).

Respect the layered threat but don't loiter naked in the WEZ. MeGaTron spent 103s in the ring firing nothing and Blacksky 161s pressing to 27.8nm — WEZ time must buy a result or you stay outside it, as Moataz, Neo and Sword correctly did (0s in WEZ).

Formation and rejoin standards were unacceptable — rejoins of 1210s/1659s/508s and 'none' formation 59-69% of the time. Wingmen owe sub-30s rejoins and continuous position. Separately, Hema's 24-32G instant flags must be investigated as a possible airframe/sensor or overcontrol issue before flying again.

operations.name: Basic Surface Attack | Tactical Pattern
operations.narrative: A five-ship CCIP range sortie flying the briefed tactical pattern (2000 ft AGL / 375 kts, accelerating to 420 kts and 500 ft AGL before pop-up), tasked with four dive-bombing runs and four BDU-50LD releases each. Sword led by example: 4-for-4 shacks, avg CEP 6.3 m, best 2.7 m, every release above 2600 ft AGL — a genuine A-grade demonstration of a stable pop, roll-in and pickle. Hema showed the potential with two shacks including a 3.5 m gem on run 3, but bracketed the target 18–19 m short-right on runs 2 and 4 and — critically — released at 1224 and 1387 ft AGL, inside the Mk-82-class frag envelope. Blacksky did not shack a single pass yet flew the most instructive scoreboard of the day: a clean tightening trend from 37 m down to the high teens, with an unmistakable 16–19 m LEFT bias on every drop, a classic wind/sight-picture correction he can dial out overnight. Megatron owns the extremes — a beautiful 3.3 m shack on run 2 sitting between 32 m and 33 m throwaways, and all four deliveries flown 30–80 kts slow of the briefed pop speed. The bright news: nobody jettisoned bombs; the tracker shows all four pilots with CCIP passes pickled all four rounds, so the six bombs returned on the blocks are consistent with a 4-ship dropping 16 total minus the wingman shortfalls — no jettison penalty was applied because no jettison event appears in the data. Mazen (slot 4, tracker name ToRnAdO) delivered nothing: zero resolved passes, and a string of eleven HIGH_G_INSTANT flags reaching 21.9 G with a 30 kt minimum speed that scream airframe departure or telemetry glitch — his emergency landing is waived per the directive, but the G-spikes are a hard flag for maintenance/replay review. Formation discipline was the flight's weak flank: only Blacksky (34 s single join, 85.6 discipline) and Sword (as lead) kept it tight, while Hema logged 20 join attempts (worst 269 s) and Megatron sat 'none' 52% of the sortie with a 747 s worst rejoin. No enemy air, no ground kills logged, and — importantly — no friendly-fire kills anywhere in the tracker; nothing here is scored as fratricide. Overall a productive accuracy range with one standout lead, two correctable-error wingmen, one no-drop, and a clear message that station keeping is lagging the bombing.
lessons: Directional miss signatures are gold: Blacksky's consistent LEFT and Hema's SHORT/RIGHT are single-axis fixes — correct the sight picture and the CEP collapses.
Fly the briefed parameters — Megatron's 340–390 kt deliveries and Hema's sub-1500 ft AGL releases both degraded the solution and, in Hema's case, busted the frag floor.
Bombing accuracy means nothing without formation discipline: rejoin under 30 seconds and stay on station — half the flight was 'none' or fighting long joins.

operations.name: Max Range GBU Drop
operations.narrative: This was a CCRP maximum-range GBU-12 laser-guided bomb sortie, and by the instructor's account the flight spent a lot of time circling before getting to business. Per the debrief, on the first run neither Sword nor Moataz released, and Hema and Blacksky held at a waypoint while Sword and Moataz ran their pass and rejoined before recovering. The tracker backs the theme: only Blacksky actually pickled, dropping two GBU-12s from 52,157 ft at 601 kts — a genuine high-altitude stand-off profile exactly in the spirit of a max-range LGB drop. Unfortunately both of Blacksky's weapons were logged BOMB_IGNORED at roughly 7.7 km, meaning the laser guidance never brought them onto the target; for LGBs that points squarely at designation — lasing timing, code match, or coordinate entry — rather than a release-parameter error. Sword flew the most polished airplane of the day at a gentle 2.7 G max and checked in first, but recorded no release and no formation telemetry at all, so his contribution to the weapons event is a miss. Moataz posted the best formation discipline in the flight (86.8) and the crispest rejoin (35 s, one attempt), but he too did not put a bomb off on the first run. Hema held as directed and showed flashes of excellent wingman work — a 5 s rejoin and 25% fingertip time — but a 738 s worst rejoin dragged his average to 192 s and tells the story of a flight that kept losing and re-forming station. Airmanship was safe across the board: no G exceedances, no deck busts (the single-digit minAGL figures are sensor artefacts against 20,000-plus-foot average altitudes), and Moataz's 5.9 G was the only mildly aggressive pull. Formation discipline scores ranged from Blacksky's 60 up to Moataz's 87, with a lot of 'none' and trail time reflecting all that circling. The recurring FORMATION_BREAK events near ±500 ft delta altitude show the pattern of stepping up and down between holds rather than tight, level station-keeping. From a training standpoint the flight rehearsed the high-altitude CCRP mechanics and the holding discipline, which is valuable, but the mission's core objective — a successful long-range guided hit — was not achieved by anyone. The good news is the trend: Blacksky and Sword are both markedly stronger than their July BFM lows, and Hema keeps climbing. The single biggest fix for next time is closing the laser-guidance loop so those stand-off releases actually track to the target.
lessons: For CCRP LGB drops, releasing the weapon is only half the job — confirm laser code match, self-lasing timing and steady designation through impact; Blacksky's two ~7.7 km 'ignored' bombs almost certainly failed on guidance, not release.

Every shooter must complete the pass: Sword and Moataz both went dry on the first run, so a max-range LGB sortie produced zero effective hits across four jets. Brief clear release responsibilities and a re-attack plan.

Rejoin consistency is a discipline, not a talent — Hema showed both a 5 s and a 738 s rejoin, and Blacksky/Hema pair took 16+ minutes to re-form. Standardise a rejoin airspeed and geometry so every join looks like the best one.

operations.name: Basic Surface Attack | Tactical Pattern
operations.narrative: This was a four-plus-ship CCIP dive-bombing range with Mk-82 slicks and a pair of MK-82AIR retards, followed by general formation work. Six pilot slots logged; the shooting was done by Sword, Blacksky, Golden, Megatron and Ibraheem, with HIsham arriving late and never getting into the game. Every man who dropped scored at least one shack on his opening pass — a good sign of solid initial setups — but consistency fell apart after the first release for most. Sword was the standout: an avgCEP of 19.2 m, a 5.6 m opening shack, and the safest deliveries on the range, every bomb pickled between 2868 and 3346 ft AGL. Blacksky was close behind at 23.6 m with a 9.1 m shack, but showed a repeatable LONG-and-LEFT bias that screams an uncorrected sight picture or wind offset. Golden earned respect for the best learning curve of the day, walking his CEP down 40.7 → 17.6 → 11.4 m to finish on a shack. The formation picture, however, was messy. Golden and Megatron between them logged over 1800 formation flags, spent roughly a fifth to a quarter of the sortie in 'none', and each posted a rejoin near or over 2.5 minutes (177 s and 148 s) — that is a lost wingman, not a rejoin. Ibraheem was the mirror image: the tightest formation flying of the flight (fingertip 65%, discipline 89.9) but the worst and most dangerous bombing — two frag-envelope busts at 1257 and 1013 ft AGL plus wild release gates (9° dive at 483 kts, then 599 kts). His 8.07 G pull also nudged past the training gate. No air-to-air, no ground kills confirmed by tracker, and zero friendly kills — the formation breaks were airmanship failures, not collisions. Overall the flight can shoot but needs to decide whether it wants to be accurate or safe, then do both at once. Priority fixes: hard-floor discipline on release altitude, kill the directional aim biases, and tighten rejoins to under 30 seconds.

Directional miss signatures are diagnostic: Blacksky's repeated LONG/LEFT and the flight-wide SHORT tendency are correctable sight-picture/wind errors, not bad luck.
A wingman who takes 148-177 seconds to rejoin is combat-ineffective; Golden and Megatron need to fly formation position, not chase it back after wandering off.
